title: Let Teenagers Fail (a Little)
paragraphs: When my niece forgot her science project on the kitchen table last month, my sister drove forty minutes to the school to deliver it. I understand the impulse. If I were a parent, I would probably do the same. Yet I believe this kind of rescue, repeated every week, does teenagers more harm than good.

Psychologists who study adolescence often say that young people learn resilience by solving small problems on their own. If nobody had ever let me miss a bus, I would never have learned to check the timetable. My first failed exam taught me more about studying than ten lectures about it. Had my teacher changed the mark out of kindness, I would have kept studying badly.

A friend of mine teaches at a secondary school in Puebla. She told me that the students who struggle most at university are often the best ones in class. They have rarely made a serious mistake, so their first one feels like a disaster. 'They freeze,' she said. 'They have no experience of recovering.' Her observation is only one person's, of course, but it matches what I have seen myself.

Some parents argue that the world is more competitive than it used to be, so children cannot afford mistakes. That sounds reasonable, but it is easy to overlook something important. Employers rarely ask whether a candidate has never failed; they want to know how that person reacts when things go wrong. A teenager who has been protected from every disappointment has had no chance to practise.

Of course, I am not suggesting that adults should disappear. A parent who watches from a distance, ready to listen, is very different from one who solves everything in advance. The first approach says, 'I trust you.' The second, however kind it may be, says, 'I don't think you can manage.'

So next time your son leaves his lunch at home, consider letting him go hungry until the afternoon. It will be uncomfortable for both of you, but he will remember to pack it tomorrow. And if he doesn't, well, that is another lesson waiting to be learned. Failure, in small and safe doses, is not the opposite of education. It is part of it.

title: The Women Who Mend the Nets
paragraphs: At six in the morning, the small cove near Talcahuano, on Chile's southern coast, is already noisy. Boats are unloaded, boxes are filled with ice, and gulls circle above the pier. Fewer people look at the quiet corner behind the fish shed, where a group of women sit with enormous green nets across their knees.

Marta Opazo, sixty-one, has repaired nets for thirty-five years. 'Every hole has to be found with your fingers, not your eyes,' she explains, pulling a thick plastic needle through the mesh. A badly mended net can cost a fisherman a whole day's catch, so the work is taken very seriously. Marta is paid by the metre, and on a good week she earns about ninety thousand pesos.

The job used to be passed from mother to daughter. Today, however, few young people want it. The hours are long, the pay is modest, and the damp cold gets into your bones. Marta's own daughter works in a bank in Concepción, and Marta says she has no regrets about that. 'I wanted her to sit in an office,' she says. 'I never wanted her to sit here.'

Yet the trade may not disappear after all. Last year a local cooperative began teaching a short course to anyone aged sixteen to thirty. Students are shown how to read damage, tie the traditional knots and calculate the price of a repair. Twelve people have finished the course so far, and three of them are now employed by the cooperative.

One of them is Joaquín Vera, who is eighteen. He admits he joined because he needed money, not because he loved the sea. 'But after a month I started to notice things,' he says. 'You hear the whole harbour from here: the engines, the jokes, the arguments about football. It's a bit like sitting in the middle of a village.'

Marta watches him work and nods without saying much. For her, that is the highest praise. Nets, she reminds me, were being mended on this shore long before the road was built, and she does not believe the habit will end with her. 'If he stays another five years,' she says with a smile, 'I might even let him use my needle.'

title: Review: The Salt Road
paragraphs: Few films begin as quietly as The Salt Road, the debut feature from Argentine director Inés Calvo. For the first ten minutes, nothing happens except that a lorry crosses a white desert. Some viewers will be tempted to look at their phones. They should resist, because those ten minutes teach us how to watch everything that follows.

The story is simple. Aurelio, a retired lorry driver played with remarkable restraint by Ramón Ibáñez, agrees to take his granddaughter Luz across the salt flats of northern Argentina to see her mother, whom she hasn't met for six years. Neither of them wants to talk about why. Luz, sixteen and furious, spends most of the journey with her headphones on.

What makes the film special is what it leaves out. We are never told what happened between Luz's mother and grandfather; we have to piece it together from a broken cassette, an unsent letter and a single, painful dinner at a roadside café. Some critics have called this frustrating. I found it deeply respectful of the audience.

The soundtrack is equally restrained. Instead of a conventional score, the director uses the noise of the engine, the wind and the occasional folk song from the radio. The silence between them is just as important as the music. In one memorable scene, Aurelio turns the radio off in the middle of a song, and the sudden quiet says more than any dialogue could.

The cinematography deserves every prize it has won. Cameraman Diego Salas shoots the landscape as though it were an ocean, and the dazzling white ground makes the characters look small and slightly lost. Unfortunately, the second half loses momentum. A subplot about a mechanic in a small village adds little, and the final scene, while moving, arrives about twenty minutes too late.

Still, these are minor complaints. The Salt Road is not a film for those who want fast action, but it rewards patience generously. It asks what we owe to family members who have hurt us, and it wisely refuses to give a simple answer. It runs for one hour and fifty minutes, and I did not check the time once. Four stars out of five. Take a friend, and prepare to talk about it afterwards.

title: Whistle and Wisdom: A Young Referee Speaks
paragraphs: Tatiane Moura is twenty-six and referees youth and amateur football matches in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. She spoke to us after a Sunday tournament about nerves, abuse from the stands and why she thinks every teenager should try refereeing once.
Q: Why did you become a referee?

A: Honestly, by accident. When I was seventeen, I played in a girls' league, and one day the referee didn't turn up. The coach pushed a whistle into my hand and said, 'You know the rules better than anyone.' I was terrified, but I loved it. I was paid thirty reais that day, just enough for lunch, and I have never stopped.
Q: What is the hardest part of the job?

A: The shouting. Some parents forget that the players are children. Last season a father told me that I had ruined his son's career, and the boy was only eleven. At first I took it personally. Now I breathe slowly, look at the nearest tree and remember that I cannot control other people's behaviour, only my own decisions.
Q: Do you ever make mistakes?

A: Every match. The key is not to pretend otherwise. If I realise I was wrong, I tell the players at half-time. They are surprisingly forgiving when you are honest, and, more importantly, they stop trying to cheat me.
Q: Has refereeing changed you outside football?

A: Completely. I used to avoid arguments at all costs. Now I can make an unpopular decision calmly and explain it politely. At university, my classmates say I'm the one they ask when a group project goes wrong, because I don't take sides.
Q: What would you say to a teenager who is thinking about trying it?

A: Do it, even if you only referee a few matches. You will understand the game differently, and you will respect referees more. Besides, it is one of the few jobs where you must be honest in front of two hundred people. If you can do that, an exam or a job interview will feel easy. I'm not saying it's comfortable, but it is certainly worth it.

title: The Quiet Return of Handwriting
paragraphs: Ten years ago, many predicted that handwriting would vanish within a generation. Keyboards were faster, screens were everywhere, and schools in several countries reduced the time spent on joined-up letters. Yet in recent years, something unexpected has happened: stationery shops are doing well, and notebooks, fountain pens and planners are being bought by people who grew up with smartphones.

Why? One explanation is practical. Several studies suggest that students who take notes by hand tend to remember concepts better than those who type, perhaps because writing slowly forces them to choose what matters. Typists, by contrast, often copy lecturers word for word without really thinking.

However, I believe the appeal goes beyond efficiency. A handwritten note has a personality that no font can imitate. When my grandmother sends me a card, I can recognise her slanting letters before I open the envelope, and I know she paused to think, because there is a small crossed-out word in the second line. That visible effort is part of the message.

A teacher I know in Santiago asks her students to write the first draft of every essay by hand. At first they complain, she says, but after a few weeks they admit that their ideas are clearer. 'The paper doesn't offer them a thousand distractions,' she told me.

Critics argue that this is simple nostalgia, and they may be partly right. Nobody should be forced to write an essay by hand if they have a physical difficulty, and there is no reason to ban keyboards from classrooms. Typing is an essential skill, and it will remain so. The question is not which tool is better, but which one suits which task.

A balanced approach is therefore the most sensible. Draft your ideas on paper, where mistakes are cheap and nobody can interrupt you with a notification. Then move to the screen to edit, share and store. Used together, the two methods complement each other rather than compete.

Perhaps that explains the quiet comeback. People have not rejected technology; they have simply realised that slowing down occasionally is a form of freedom. In a world that rewards speed, a pen may be the most radical tool on the desk.

title: The Last Bus to Cuenca
paragraphs: The last bus from Guayaquil to Cuenca left at nine, and Daniela had missed it by exactly two minutes. She stood on the platform with her backpack and a plastic bag of empanadas, watching the red lights shrink into the darkness. Her brother's wedding was the next morning at eleven. She had promised to read the speech.

The ticket seller, a tired man with grey hair, gave a shrug. 'Nothing until five,' he said. 'There is a truck driver who sometimes takes passengers for twenty dollars, but I wouldn't recommend it.' Daniela counted her money. She had twenty-four dollars, a phone with six per cent battery and a speech she hadn't finished.

She was still deciding when a small white car stopped outside the station. The window came down, and a young woman looked out. 'Cuenca?' she asked. 'My cousin saw you running. I'm going there tonight, and the road is long when you're alone.' Daniela hesitated. Her mother had always warned her never to get into cars with strangers, and yet the woman's smile seemed sincere.

'Let me send my friend your name and the number plate,' Daniela said. The woman laughed. 'Good idea. I would do the same.' Daniela photographed the plate, sent it to her friend Carolina, and climbed in. They drove through the mountains in a comfortable silence, with the heater on and the radio low.

Around midnight, the woman, whose name was Verónica, began to talk. She was a nurse, and she was driving to Cuenca because her father had been taken to hospital that afternoon. 'I haven't told anyone yet that I'm frightened,' she admitted. Daniela, who had spent the evening feeling sorry for herself, suddenly felt rather small. She took out her notebook, tore out the unfinished speech and, for the next hour, simply listened.

They reached Cuenca at three. Verónica dropped her at a small hostel and refused any money, asking only for her number 'to know you arrived safely'. Hours later, standing in front of eighty relatives, Daniela put her notes aside. 'Marcos,' she said, looking at her brother, 'I nearly missed this day. On the way here I learned that people we have never met can be unexpectedly kind. I hope you and Elena will be that kind to each other.' Afterwards, her phone buzzed with a message from an unknown number: 'Papá is better. Congratulations to your brother. V.'

title: Waste Audit at Colegio Andino
paragraphs: ## Introduction

This report presents the results of a one-week waste audit carried out by the Environmental Club of Colegio Andino in Arequipa, Peru. The aim was to find out how much rubbish the school produces, and how much of it could be recycled.
## Method

During one school week in May, students emptied every bin in the cafeteria, the classrooms and the playground each afternoon. Each session was supervised by a teacher to make sure the bins were handled safely. The waste was sorted into five categories: paper, plastic, food, glass and other. Each category was weighed on a kitchen scale borrowed from the cooking classroom, and the figures were recorded in a table. Because the scale was not very accurate, the results should be considered approximate.
## Findings

In total, about 212 kilograms of waste were collected. Food made up the largest share, at roughly 40 per cent, followed by paper at 28 per cent and plastic at 21 per cent. Glass and other waste together accounted for the remaining 11 per cent. Glass was almost absent, probably because few students bring drinks in glass bottles. Most of the paper was clean and dry, which means that it could have been recycled easily. By contrast, nearly all the plastic had been contaminated with food, so it was unsuitable for recycling. Surprisingly, Friday produced 30 per cent more waste than Monday, probably because of the end-of-week birthday celebrations. Students interviewed in the cafeteria said that they often throw away fruit because the portions are too big.
## Recommendations

It is recommended that the school introduce separate bins for clean paper and plastic bottles, and that the cafeteria offer smaller portions at a lower price. Moreover, a short rinsing station near the exit would help students clean their containers before throwing them away. The club estimates that the new bins would cost around 900 soles, which could be financed by selling used uniforms at the next school fair. A follow-up audit should be carried out in October to measure any improvement.
In conclusion, most of the problem seems to come from poor organisation rather than carelessness.

title: A Letter About an Unlit Bus Stop
paragraphs: Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to draw your attention to the lack of street lighting at the bus stop on Calle Hidalgo, opposite the Colegio Jalisco in Guadalajara. I am a seventeen-year-old student, and I use this stop every weekday. Since the beginning of October, the two lamps that used to illuminate it have not been working, and nothing has been done to repair them.

As I finish my after-school classes at half past six, I often wait for the bus in complete darkness. The nearest alternative is a fifteen-minute walk through unlit streets. Last Tuesday, a man tried to take a classmate's phone, and she was only able to escape because a shop owner heard her shouting. Fortunately, she was not hurt, but several students now refuse to take the bus after dark, and some are asking their parents to collect them by car.

I reported the problem twice through the city's telephone line, on 8 and 22 October. On both occasions I was told that a technician would be sent within a week. However, none has appeared. Neither time was I given a reference number, which makes it impossible to follow up. I would therefore appreciate it if you could explain why the repair has been delayed.

Moreover, I would like to suggest two further measures. Firstly, a cheap solar lamp could be installed temporarily while the original lights are repaired. Secondly, the stop could be included in the council's night-time safety patrols, which, I understand, already cover the main avenue two streets away. Had these measures been taken earlier, the incident last Tuesday might have been avoided.

I would be grateful for a written reply within fifteen working days. If the matter is not resolved by then, my classmates and I intend to collect signatures and present them at the next public meeting. We would, however, prefer to cooperate with you rather than complain. A copy of this letter has been sent to the school principal.
Thank you for your time and attention.
Yours faithfully,
Ximena Duarte

title: Why I Support the Tourist Tax
paragraphs: Last summer I spent a week in Lisbon, and I loved it. I also spent about two hours in a queue to ride a famous yellow tram, and I felt guilty the whole time. The residents behind me, who only wanted to get home, were being slowed down by hundreds of tourists, myself included.

That is why I support the tourist tax that several European cities now charge. In Lisbon, visitors pay a small fee for each night of their stay, which is added to the hotel bill. Some travellers complain loudly. Yet the amount is usually a few euros per person, a tiny fraction of what most visitors spend on meals and souvenirs.

Opponents say the tax is unfair because it punishes visitors for coming. I disagree. Tourism does bring money, but it also brings costs: more rubbish, more pressure on public transport, and rent that rises because owners prefer to let a flat to visitors. In some neighbourhoods, young people born in the area can no longer afford to stay. These costs are paid by everyone who lives there, whereas many of the profits go to a small number of businesses.

A fair tax, in other words, does not punish tourists; it asks them to contribute to the city that they enjoy. The important condition is that the money must be spent visibly. If visitors see that their euros are being used to repair the pavement, clean beaches or keep museums open, resentment will fall on both sides.

Of course, a tax alone will not solve everything. Although it may reduce the number of cheap, short stays, it will not stop crowded squares. Cities also need limits on short-term rentals and better planning for popular districts. Nevertheless, it is a reasonable first step, and one that asks little from each traveller.

I will return to Lisbon, and next time I will happily pay my fee. I might even walk up the hill instead of waiting two hours for the tram. My legs, and the people behind me in the queue, will thank me. Being a good guest, after all, means thinking about the host.
